questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state how the first-order half-life depends on concentration
questions.stem: Two runs of the same first-order reaction are started at different concentrations. What happens to the half-life in the more concentrated run?

options.text: It is unchanged, because a first-order half-life does not depend on the starting concentration
It is longer, because a higher concentration leaves more reactant for the reaction to consume
options.misconception: believes more starting material must lengthen a first-order half-life

options.text: It is shorter, because a higher concentration pushes the reaction forward more quickly
options.misconception: believes the initial rate sets the time taken for each halving

options.text: It is longer, because the rate of a first-order reaction falls as the reaction proceeds
options.misconception: uses the falling rate of a first-order run to predict its half-life

questions.explanation: The half-life of a first-order reaction is 0.693 divided by the rate constant, and the rate constant depends only on temperature and the presence of a catalyst, so every run of the reaction has the same half-life however it was started. The rate does fall as a first-order run proceeds, but it falls by the same proportion each half-life, which is exactly why the time for each halving is constant. Contrast a second-order reaction, whose half-life of 1 over k times the starting concentration grows as the run is made more dilute.
questions.hint: Ask what the half-life expression contains: a rate constant, or a concentration too?

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify the step that controls the rate of a mechanism
questions.stem: A proposed mechanism has a slow first step followed by a fast second step. Which step controls the rate that is actually observed?

options.text: The slow first step, because the fast step cannot run faster than it is supplied
The fast second step, because it completes more of the reaction each second
options.misconception: believes the quickest step sets the pace of the whole mechanism

options.text: Both steps added together, because every step contributes equally to the rate
options.misconception: believes the rate is the sum of the rates of all the steps

options.text: The number of steps, because a two-step mechanism always runs twice as fast as a one-step mechanism
options.misconception: believes step count rather than step speed sets the rate

questions.explanation: The overall rate of a multi-step mechanism is set by its slowest, rate-determining step, because every later step must consume the intermediate that step produces. A fast second step can only work as fast as material arrives. This matters when writing a rate law from a mechanism, since the slow elementary step fixes the order in the rate expression and the fast steps usually do not appear in it.
questions.hint: The observed rate cannot beat the pace at which material is supplied.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: interpret the temperature dependence of a rate constant
questions.stem: One reaction has a rate constant of 4.0 x 10^-3 per s at 290 K and a larger value at 310 K. What does that change establish?

options.text: The activation energy is positive, because the rate constant rises as the temperature rises
The activation energy is negative, because the rate constant fell as the temperature rose
options.misconception: reads a rise in the rate constant as a fall

options.text: The activation energy is zero, because the temperature change had no effect at all
options.misconception: believes an unchanged rate constant implies no barrier

options.text: The activation energy is positive, because the mechanism must have changed on heating
options.misconception: credits a mechanism change rather than a lower fraction crossing the barrier

questions.explanation: The Arrhenius relation makes the logarithm of the rate constant rise linearly as the reciprocal temperature falls, and that pattern only happens when the activation energy is positive. A positive activation energy is the normal case, since molecules must climb an energy barrier before reacting, and heating shifts a larger fraction of them across it. A rate constant that rose with temperature is exactly the evidence that such a barrier exists.
questions.hint: Consider whether molecules must climb a barrier before they can react.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: decide which species belong in an equilibrium constant
questions.stem: A heterogeneous system contains a solid chunk, a pure liquid and three dissolved species. Which species appear in the equilibrium constant expression?

options.text: The three dissolved species only, because solids and pure liquids are left out
All five species, because every reactant and product belongs in the expression
options.misconception: believes every species must be listed no matter what its phase

options.text: The solid and the pure liquid only, because they set the rate of exchange
options.misconception: keeps the phases that are actually left out of the expression

options.text: The three dissolved species and the solid, but not the pure liquid
options.misconception: includes one pure phase while excluding the other without reason

questions.explanation: The expression is written only for species whose concentration can change, so dissolved species and gases appear and pure solids and pure liquids do not. Those two phases have a fixed activity that is folded into the constant, which is why removing some solid from a saturated solution does not shift the equilibrium while removing dissolved product does. A gas is not exempt, since its pressure does vary and gases do appear.
questions.hint: Ask which of the species has a concentration that can actually vary.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: name the three stresses that shift an equilibrium
questions.stem: Which set lists the three kinds of stress that shift the position of an equilibrium?

options.text: Changing a concentration, changing the volume or pressure, and changing the temperature
Changing a concentration, adding a catalyst, and changing the temperature
options.misconception: counts a catalyst as a stress even though it changes no equilibrium

options.text: Changing the volume, adding a catalyst, and changing the pressure only
options.misconception: counts a catalyst twice through volume and pressure

options.text: Changing the temperature, changing a concentration, and adding an inert gas at fixed volume
options.misconception: counts an inert gas as a stress, but at fixed volume it alters no partial pressure

questions.explanation: The three recognised stresses are a change in concentration, a change in volume or pressure, and a change in temperature, and each of those shifts the position of the system. A catalyst is not among them, because it speeds both directions equally and leaves the position untouched. An inert gas added at fixed volume is also not one, because none of the reacting partial pressures changes when the volume stays the same.
questions.hint: A stress must change a reacting concentration, a reacting pressure, or the temperature.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state which change alters the equilibrium constant
questions.stem: A sealed vessel holds an exothermic equilibrium and is then heated. What happens to K for the exothermic direction?

options.text: It falls, and temperature is the only change that alters K at all
It stays fixed, because every equilibrium keeps the same constant whatever happens
options.misconception: believes K is immune to any change in the surroundings

options.text: It rises, because the system has to absorb some of the added heat
options.misconception: applies the endothermic case to a reaction that gives out heat

options.text: It changes only when the volume changes, and never when the temperature changes
options.misconception: believes pressure rather than temperature is the only thing that moves K

questions.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic direction, and since the forward direction here is exothermic, heating drives the system back towards the reactants, so the forward constant falls. Concentration and volume changes move the position of the system while leaving K untouched, so temperature is the only one of the three stresses that alters the constant itself. That is why an exothermic reaction yields more product at a lower temperature.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the added heat favours, then read off the constant for the exothermic direction.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: classify an equilibrium by its phases
questions.stem: A sealed vessel holds a solid in contact with the solution it has partly dissolved in. How is the resulting equilibrium classified?

options.text: Heterogeneous, because the reacting species do not all occupy the same phase
Homogeneous, because every species is inside one sealed vessel
options.misconception: equates one container with one phase

options.text: Heterogeneous, because the vessel is sealed rather than open to the air
options.misconception: equates a sealed container with a second phase

options.text: Homogeneous, because only the dissolved ions take part in the equilibrium
options.misconception: ignores the solid phase that is part of the equilibrium

questions.explanation: The classification rests on the phases present, not on the container. A solid in contact with its own dissolved ions gives two phases, so the equilibrium is heterogeneous, and that is exactly why the solid is left out of the equilibrium expression. If the same species reacted entirely in a single solution, with no solid present, the equilibrium would be homogeneous and the solid would be absent from the question rather than from the expression.
questions.hint: Count the phases in contact, not the number of vessels.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify what raises buffer capacity
questions.stem: Two buffers hold the same acid to conjugate base ratio at pH 4.76, but one is ten times more concentrated. Which resists added acid or added base better?

options.text: The more concentrated one, because more of both buffer components are there to react
The more dilute one, because dilute solutions damp pH swings more easily
options.misconception: believes dilution improves a buffer rather than exhausting it

options.text: Both resist equally, because capacity depends only on the ratio of acid to base
options.misconception: believes the ratio alone fixes the capacity

options.text: The more concentrated one, because its pH must sit closer to seven
options.misconception: ties capacity to the pH value rather than to the amounts present

questions.explanation: Two things fix a buffer's behaviour: the ratio of acid to conjugate base sets the pH, and the total concentration of both partners sets the capacity. A ten-fold increase in concentration gives ten times as much of each component to neutralise an addition, so the same dose of acid or base moves the pH far less. Capacity is greatest when the two components are present in similar amounts, and a buffer that is far too dilute runs out quickly.
questions.hint: Separate in your mind the ratio, which sets pH, from the amounts, which set capacity.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of adding a common ion on solubility
questions.stem: A saturated silver chloride solution is made richer in chloride by adding sodium chloride. What happens to the solid?

options.text: Its molar solubility falls, while the solubility product stays the same at a fixed temperature
Its molar solubility rises, because the added chloride pushes more dissolution
options.misconception: reads an added product as a push towards dissolving more solid

options.text: Its solubility product rises, because the added chloride becomes a new product species
options.misconception: believes the constant absorbs the change in concentrations

options.text: Nothing changes, because a solid cannot be affected by anything in solution
options.misconception: believes a solid phase is immune to solution composition

questions.explanation: The solubility product holds at a fixed temperature whatever the concentrations are, and adding chloride raises the chloride concentration, so the silver ion concentration must fall to keep the product constant. The saturated solution therefore holds less dissolved solid, and some of it precipitates, which is the common-ion effect. A drop in solubility at unchanged K is exactly the pattern to expect, not a rise.
questions.hint: Keep the product constant and ask what must happen to one factor when the other rises.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: locate the equivalence point on a titration curve
questions.stem: A curve of pH against volume of added titrant is recorded while an acid is neutralised by a base. Where does the equivalence point sit?

options.text: Where the moles of added base equal the moles of acid, marked by the steepest rise
Where the pH first begins to climb at all from its starting value
options.misconception: takes the first response of the curve for the end point

options.text: Where the pH reaches exactly seven, in every titration that is run
options.misconception: assumes a universal neutral pH regardless of the acid titrated

options.text: Halfway up the vertical rise, where the curve becomes a straight line
options.misconception: confuses the middle of the steep section with the equivalence point

questions.explanation: The equivalence point is where titrant and analyte have reacted in exactly equal amounts, and on the curve it shows up as the inflection in the steep section, the region of near-vertical rise. The pH there is not generally seven: a strong acid with a strong base gives seven, while a weak acid with a strong base gives a value above seven because of the conjugate base formed. Halfway up the rise is a different point, and for a weak acid it is where the pH equals the pKa.
questions.hint: Tie the position to equal moles, then to the shape of the curve rather than to a fixed pH.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compare the titration curves of a strong and a weak acid
questions.stem: A strong monoprotic acid and a weak monoprotic acid of equal concentration are each titrated with the same base. Which difference appears early in the two curves?

options.text: The strong acid starts at a lower pH and shows no buffer region
The weak acid starts at a lower pH and shows no buffer region
options.misconception: swaps the two behaviours, which is the reverse of the chemistry

options.text: Both curves start at the same pH, because equal concentrations force equal acidity
options.misconception: believes concentration alone fixes the starting pH

options.text: The strong acid shows a buffer region, because it dissociates completely in water
options.misconception: believes full dissociation creates a conjugate pair to buffer with

questions.explanation: A strong monoprotic acid dissociates essentially completely, so the same concentration puts far more hydrogen ions in solution and the curve begins at a lower pH. A weak acid dissociates only partly, and as titrant is added some of it is converted to its conjugate base, giving the shallow buffer region that a strong acid never shows. The two curves converge to similar shapes near the equivalence point, which is why the early part of each curve is the diagnostic part.
questions.hint: Ask what concentration of hydrogen ions each acid actually produces at the start.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify the ion responsible for the pH of a salt solution
questions.stem: A solution of sodium ethanoate is prepared in water. Which ion accounts for its basic pH?

options.text: The ethanoate ion, which is the conjugate base of a weak acid and takes a proton from water
The sodium ion, which is the conjugate base of a strong acid and takes a proton
options.misconception: believes a cation from a strong base can remove a proton

options.text: The ethanoate ion, which is the conjugate acid of a weak base and gives up a proton
options.misconception: calls the anion a conjugate acid rather than a conjugate base

options.text: The sodium ion, which hydrolyses because a metal cation always reacts with water
options.misconception: believes any metal cation hydrolyses, ignoring its charge and pairing

questions.explanation: The ion that hydrolyses is the one that is the conjugate of a weak partner. Ethanoate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it is a weak base itself and pulls a proton from water, leaving hydroxide behind and raising the pH. The sodium ion is the conjugate of a strong base, so it has no tendency to accept a proton and stays as a spectator, which is why salts of strong bases with weak acids are basic.
questions.hint: Look for the ion whose partner in its parent acid or base is weak.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state the second law in terms of total entropy
questions.stem: Which statement expresses the second law of thermodynamics as it applies to a spontaneous change?

options.text: The total entropy of the system plus its surroundings increases for a spontaneous change
The entropy of the system alone always increases for a spontaneous change
options.misconception: believes the system must disorder itself whenever anything happens

options.text: The entropy of the surroundings always increases for a spontaneous change
options.misconception: believes the surroundings always gain entropy, which fails for an endothermic change

options.text: The total entropy stays exactly fixed for any change carried out at constant temperature
options.misconception: believes the total entropy is conserved, which is a statement about an ideal reversible path

questions.explanation: The second law is a statement about the sum, not about the system alone. For a spontaneous process the total entropy of the system and its surroundings rises, which is why a process can be spontaneous even when the system itself becomes more ordered, as long as the surroundings gain more entropy than the system loses. That is also why heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, and why a total entropy that would fall signals a process that cannot run on its own.
questions.hint: The law concerns the combination of system and surroundings.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state the significant figure rule for a pH
questions.stem: A hydrogen ion concentration is known to three significant figures, 3.16 x 10^-3 mol per L, and its pH is to be reported. How many decimal places should that pH carry?

options.text: Two, because the number of pH decimals equals the significant figures in the concentration
Three, because a pH should show the same number of decimals as the measured concentration
options.misconception: counts the pH digits instead of the digits of the concentration

options.text: Four, because a logarithm always adds one decimal place to the count of significant figures
options.misconception: believes logarithms inflate precision by a decimal place

options.text: One, because any logarithm can only ever be reported to a single decimal place
options.misconception: believes logarithms admit only one digit after the point

questions.explanation: The rule follows from the fact that the significant figures of a concentration appear as the decimal places of its logarithm, because the mantissa carries the precision. Three significant figures in 3.16 x 10^-3 mol per L therefore gives three decimals in the pH, that is 2.500. This is the mirror image of the rule for logarithms in the other direction, where digits after the decimal point of a logarithm become significant figures in the antilogarithm.
questions.hint: Convert the measured concentration to its logarithm and count where the precision lands.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state what a mean bond enthalpy can and cannot give
questions.stem: A mean bond enthalpy is tabulated as an average for one bond type taken over many compounds. What follows from that status?

options.text: It gives an estimate of a reaction enthalpy, not an exact value for one specific reaction
It gives the exact enthalpy of breaking that bond in every compound that contains it
options.misconception: believes an averaged figure applies exactly to each individual compound

options.text: It is measured directly for each compound, so no bond bookkeeping is needed at all
options.misconception: believes average values come from direct per-compound measurement

options.text: It equals the bond energy of that bond in the gas phase of one named molecule
options.misconception: confuses an average over many compounds with a single specific measurement

questions.explanation: A mean bond enthalpy is an average over many compounds, because a given bond type sits in slightly different surroundings each time, so the true figure varies from molecule to molecule. Using it to estimate a reaction enthalpy by subtracting the bonds made from the bonds broken is therefore accurate only to a few kilojoules per mole, which is usually good enough to predict a sign or a feasibility but not to replace calorimetry. The bond count and the identity of the bonds, not their precise values, drive the calculation.
questions.hint: An average cannot be exact for every member of the set it averages.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state how voltages and currents combine in the two arrangements
questions.stem: Three resistors are connected across a battery in one case in series and in another case in parallel. Which statement is correct?

options.text: In series the voltages add while the current is the same, in parallel the currents add while the voltage is the same
In series the currents add while the voltage is the same, in parallel the voltages add
options.misconception: reverses both additivity rules for the two arrangements

options.text: In both arrangements the equivalent resistance is the sum of the resistances
options.misconception: believes the same rule serves both arrangements

options.text: In parallel each branch carries the full current, so the total current is unchanged
options.misconception: believes a parallel network draws no more current than one branch

questions.explanation: Series and parallel are mirror images of each other. In series there is one path, so the same current passes through every resistor while the supply voltage is shared out among them, which is why the resistances add. In parallel each branch spans the full supply, so the voltage across each resistor is the same and the branch currents add, which is why the reciprocal resistances add instead.
questions.hint: Count the paths: one path means one current, many paths mean one voltage.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute the fraction remaining after multiple half-lives
questions.stem: A first-order reaction is allowed to run for three and a half half-lives. What fraction of the starting reactant remains? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Each half-life multiplies the amount by one half, so three and a half half-lives multiply it by 0.5 cubed times the square root of 0.5, which is 0.125 times 0.7071, that is 0.0884. Treating three and a half as three gives 0.125, and treating it as four gives 0.0625, so the half must be handled as an exponent of one half rather than rounded away.
questions.hint: Write the fraction as a power of one half and evaluate the half power.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Time for a given extent of reaction
questions.learningObjective: find the time for a first-order reaction to reach a given extent
questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0450 per minute. How many minutes are needed for 90 percent of the starting reactant to be used up?
questions.explanation: Ninety percent used up leaves one tenth, so the time is the natural log of 10 divided by the rate constant, which is 2.3026 over 0.0450, that is 51.2 minutes. Using the log of 9 instead of 10 would use the fraction of the original rather than the fraction remaining, and using the log of 0.90 in the numerator gives a negative time, which flags the wrong ratio immediately.
questions.hint: The ratio that enters the integrated law is starting amount over amount remaining.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: apply the integrated second-order law
questions.stem: A second-order reaction in one reactant has a rate constant of 0.180 L per mol per s and starts at 0.200 mol per L. What is the reactant concentration after 30.0 s?
questions.explanation: The integrated second-order law gives one over the concentration as kt plus one over the starting concentration, so the reciprocal is 0.180 times 30.0 plus 5.00, that is 10.4 L per mol, and the concentration is 0.0962 mol per L. Using the first-order expression instead would give 0.201 mol per L, essentially unchanged, because an exponential cannot describe a second-order run.
questions.hint: The reciprocal of the concentration, not the concentration, is what varies linearly.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Time for a second-order concentration drop
questions.learningObjective: apply the integrated second-order law to a target concentration
questions.stem: In a run that is second order in one reactant, the rate constant is 0.120 L per mol per s and the starting concentration is 0.250 mol per L. How many seconds are needed for the concentration to fall to one third of that starting value?
questions.explanation: One third of 0.250 mol per L is 0.0833 mol per L, and the integrated law gives t as the difference in the reciprocals divided by k, so the reciprocal of 0.0833 minus the reciprocal of 0.250 is 12.0 minus 4.0, that is 8.0 L per mol, and dividing by 0.120 gives 66.7 s. Taking the ratio of the concentrations as three rather than inverting it gives a negative answer, which is the quickest way to spot the slip.
questions.hint: Invert both concentrations, subtract, then divide by the rate constant.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Rate constant at a new temperature
questions.learningObjective: extrapolate a rate constant to a new temperature
questions.stem: A reaction has a rate constant of 4.0 x 10^-3 per s at 290 K and an activation energy of 75.0 kJ per mol. Using R = 8.314 J per mol per K, what is the rate constant at 310 K? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The Arrhenius relation gives k at the new temperature as the old constant times the exponential of minus Ea over R times the difference in reciprocal temperatures, and the reciprocal difference is negative, so the exponential is a growth factor of about 7.44, giving 0.0298 per s. Leaving the activation energy in kilojoules while R is in joules makes the exponent tiny and the answer almost unchanged from the starting value, which is the usual silent error here.
questions.hint: Convert the activation energy to joules before dividing by R.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate an equilibrium constant from measured concentrations
questions.stem: At equilibrium a vessel holds 0.0500 mol per L of product and 0.100 mol per L each of the two reactants in the reaction A plus B giving C. What is the equilibrium constant? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The expression is the product concentration over the product of the two reactant concentrations, so 0.0500 over 0.100 times 0.100 is 5.00. Adding the reactant concentrations instead of multiplying them gives a different figure, and including the product in the denominator would invert the whole ratio, which is the single most common structural error in these expressions.
questions.hint: Products go on top and reactants go below, and reactants multiply.

Writing A to the first power gives 0.40, and inverting the ratio gives 0.50, so the exponent and the position of the ratio both have to be right.

questions.topic: Pressure constant from a concentration constant
questions.learningObjective: convert a concentration constant to a pressure constant
questions.stem: For the gas reaction 2SO3 giving 2SO2 plus O2, the concentration constant is 1.50 x 10^-2 at 500 K. Using R = 0.08206 L atm per mol K, what is the pressure constant at that temperature?
questions.explanation: The pressure constant equals the concentration constant times R times T raised to the change in gaseous moles, and here products exceed reactants by one, so Kp is 1.50 x 10^-2 times 0.08206 times 500, that is 0.615. Ignoring the sign of the change in moles, or inverting the factor, gives 0.0244 or 24.4, and either error shifts the answer by orders of magnitude rather than by a few percent.

questions.learningObjective: apply the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation
questions.stem: A buffer holds its conjugate base at 0.500 times the concentration of its weak acid, and that acid has a pKa of 4.76. What pH does the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation give? Report the number only.

Taking the logarithm of the ratio the other way round adds 0.301 instead, and dropping the logarithm and simply subtracting 0.500 gives 4.26, so the value must be logged, not used raw.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: find the titrant volume needed to shift a buffer pH
questions.stem: A buffer holds 0.0500 mol of a weak acid and 0.0500 mol of its conjugate base. How many millilitres of 0.100 mol per L sodium hydroxide raise the pH by exactly 1.00 unit?
questions.explanation: A rise of one pH unit means the base to acid ratio must rise by a factor of ten, so letting x moles of hydroxide be added, 0.0500 plus x over 0.0500 minus x equals ten, which gives 11x equals 0.45 and x equals 0.0409 mol. options.misconception: believes the usual coefficient rule overrides the pure-solid exception

options.text: The dissolved ions should be left out instead, since they are spectator species
options.misconception: removes the only species whose concentrations actually vary

questions.explanation: A pure solid has an activity that does not change as long as some is present, so it is absorbed into the constant and omitted from the expression. That is why removing some of the solid from a saturated solution does not disturb the equilibrium, whereas removing dissolved product does. Including the solid would also make the constant change every time the mass of solid changes, which is not how a constant at fixed temperature behaves.
questions.hint: Ask whether the amount of that phase can change without the system changing state.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Charge and hydrolysis in a salt
questions.learningObjective: correct a mistaken neutrality claim for a salt solution
questions.stem: A student predicts that a solution of ammonium chloride is neutral, because the chloride ion comes from a strong acid. What is the flaw?

options.text: The ammonium ion is the conjugate acid of a weak base and hydrolyses, so the solution is acidic
There is no flaw, because any salt of a strong acid must give a neutral solution
options.misconception: believes one end of a salt decides the pH on its own

options.text: The student is right, and the solution is acidic only if the chloride ion hydrolyses
options.misconception: assigns the hydrolysis to the anion of a strong acid

options.text: The student chose the right ion but the wrong charge, so the charge must be balanced instead
options.misconception: treats a charge balance calculation as a substitute for hydrolysis

questions.explanation: Both ions have to be considered, and only one of them hydrolyses here. Chloride is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it is too weak a base to take a meaningful proton from water, while ammonium is the conjugate acid of a weak base and does donate a proton, leaving hydronium behind and making the solution acidic. Salts of a strong acid with a weak base are acidic, which is the mirror image of the ethanoate case.
questions.hint: Check both ions, and pick the one whose parent acid or base is weak.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify a systematic error from an ignored heat capacity
questions.stem: A student computes the heat released in a coffee-cup experiment using only the mass and the specific heat capacity of the water. What systematic error does that create?

options.text: The heat taken up by the cup is ignored, so the reported heat released is too small
The heat taken up by the cup is ignored, so the reported heat released is too large
options.misconception: gets the direction of the systematic error backwards

options.text: There is no error, because a thin cup cannot absorb a measurable amount of heat
options.misconception: believes the apparatus contributes no heat capacity at all

options.text: The specific heat capacity is applied wrongly, so the mass of water is the real error source
options.misconception: mislabels a neglected heat capacity as a specific heat mistake

questions.explanation: The surroundings that the heat enters are the water and the cup, so the heat released equals the sum of the two heat capacities times the temperature rise. Leaving the cup out takes too little heat from the surroundings and attributes too little to the reaction, so the reported value of the heat released is too small. The error is systematic rather than random, and it can be removed by determining the assembly's heat capacity from a warm-up in which a known heat is supplied.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides the water absorbs the heat as the temperature rises.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: explain the safe order of dilution steps and the reason
questions.stem: Explain why the correct laboratory procedure is to add concentrated acid slowly to a large volume of water, and never to pour water onto concentrated acid.

answer.exemplar: Diluting a concentrated acid is exothermic, so heat is released into whatever receives it. If the water is the small volume sitting on top of a large amount of acid, that few millilitres of water can absorb enough heat to boil almost at once, and the violent boiling throws corrosive acid out of the container. Adding the acid to a large excess of water instead lets the same heat spread through a much larger mass, so the temperature rise stays small, and adding it slowly with stirring keeps it small at every moment. The same logic, adding acid to water rather than water to acid, applies to the dilution of any concentrated reagent, not just acids.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: explain how an exothermic change can stop being spontaneous
questions.stem: Explain how a strongly exothermic reaction can stop being spontaneous at a high temperature, and state the criterion that decides the issue.

answer.exemplar: Spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure is decided by the Gibbs free energy change, which is the enthalpy change minus the temperature times the entropy change, not by the enthalpy change alone. An exothermic reaction has a negative enthalpy change, which favours it, but if the process also lowers the entropy of the system, then the entropy term is negative too and the minus T times S contribution opposes the enthalpy. That opposition is small at low temperature, where the enthalpy term wins and the reaction runs, and it grows in direct proportion to the temperature, so above some threshold the entropy term cancels the exothermic term, the free energy change turns positive, and the reaction is no longer spontaneous even though heat still comes out.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a solubility product determination
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how the solubility product of a sparingly soluble solid is determined. Put them in the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Substitute the measured ion concentration into the solubility product expression
Add an excess of the solid to water and stir the mixture until it is saturated
Remove the undissolved solid so that only the saturated solution is sampled
Measure the concentration of one dissolved ion in that saturated solution

questions.explanation: An excess of solid must be present first, otherwise the solution is merely unsaturated and nothing can be inferred about the product. Undissolved solid then has to be removed before sampling, because any suspended solid would carry its own undissolved material into the measurement and spoil it. Once a clean saturated sample is in hand, one ion concentration is measured, and only then can the solubility product expression be evaluated, with the pure solid correctly absent from it.
questions.hint: You cannot sample a saturated solution while solid is still floating in it.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a two-point Arrhenius calculation
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe calculating an activation energy from rate constants measured at two temperatures. Put them in the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Rearrange the two-point Arrhenius relation to solve for Ea in joules per mole
Divide the result by 1000 to report the activation energy in kilojoules per mole
Measure a rate constant k1 at temperature T1 and a rate constant k2 at a second temperature T2
Take the natural log of the ratio k2 divided by k1 for the two measurements

questions.explanation: The two rate constants and their temperatures are the raw data and must be measured before anything can be calculated from them, and both have to refer to the same mechanism. The logarithm of their ratio then appears in the rearranged relation, which is why it is taken next. The activation energy follows from substituting into that rearranged form, and it comes out in joules per mole because R is in joules, so the division by 1000 is the final and separate step for reporting in kilojoules per mole.
questions.hint: Measurements come first, the ratio is logged next, and the unit conversion is last.
